title: The First Look
scenario: You have been hired as a junior security analyst to perform an authorized assessment of Cyberflex Industries' customer portal. You have been given access to the application but no source code. Your first task is to perform reconnaissance and identify the technologies, response headers, and exposed meta-information.
objectives: Inspect HTTP response headers returned by the main application server.
Check standard search engine directives (e.g., robots.txt).
Inspect client-side HTML structure and comments for developer artifacts.
Locate the initial reconnaissance flag.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Web browsers send HTTP requests and receive response headers. Take a close look at the headers or public index page source.
hint2: Check for common information disclosure files such as /robots.txt or security headers added by the web application framework.
hint3: Check the custom HTTP header 'X-Cyberflex-Recon' returned by the home page or look at /robots.txt.

title: What's Behind the Door?
scenario: During your initial reconnaissance, you noticed indications that legacy and internal directories may still be reachable on the server. Security teams must ensure unlinked sensitive diagnostics or backups are not publicly reachable.
objectives: Review the disallow directives from your previous recon.
Navigate to hidden or unlinked administrative endpoints.
Inspect the internal system status dashboard.
Capture the internal environment flag.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Remember what you found in /robots.txt during Mission 01.
hint2: Try visiting the internal system paths listed in the robots file directly in your browser.
hint3: Visit /internal/system-status to inspect the exposed operational status report.

title: The Strange Search
scenario: The Cyberflex product search system has been behaving strangely. The development team believes the search functionality is secure. Your job is to determine whether that assumption is correct.
objectives: Investigate the product search input field.
Observe how the backend constructs database queries when submitting unexpected characters.
Perform a UNION SELECT or boolean SQL injection to extract hidden table contents.
Retrieve the confidential flag stored in the secret_vault or confidential products.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Think about how the application processes search input when single quotes (') or dashes (--) are provided.
hint2: Notice if syntax errors or all items appear when entering ' OR 1=1 -- . Check if you can combine results with a UNION query.
hint3: Try: ' UNION SELECT id, secret_name, classification, secret_value, 0, 0 FROM secret_vault -- to dump the vault!

title: A Message From Someone Else
scenario: A customer support search query and feedback reflection screen renders query strings back into the HTML without sanitization. An attacker could craft a malicious link to trick a user into executing arbitrary client-side script.
objectives: Investigate how the support ticket lookup or search term parameter is rendered in the page.
Craft an input containing HTML or script tags.
Verify that the script payload reflects directly in the DOM.
Extract the simulated session token / reflected flag.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Observe the search or ticket query parameter in the URL when searching support articles.
hint2:
Test if simple HTML tags like test or

test

render directly without escaping.
hint3: Submit a payload like or . Look at the response or trigger the triggerXss helper to retrieve the flag.

title: The Comment Nobody Sanitized
scenario: The Cyberflex customer community comments and reviews section allows users to share thoughts on products and enterprise services. Comments are persisted in the database and shown to all visitors and moderators.
objectives: Submit a comment containing benign HTML/script payloads.
Refresh the page to confirm persistent storage.
Review the simulated administrator bot review trigger.
Obtain the stored XSS validation flag.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Enter a comment with formatting tags to see if the browser parses raw HTML.
hint2: When comments are stored and re-displayed without HTML escaping, any script inside them executes every time the page loads.
hint3: Post a comment containing an XSS payload (e.g. ). The simulated review bot logs the execution and awards the flag.

title: Who Am I?
scenario: Cyberflex Industries has an administrative portal for staff. However, the login endpoint suffers from credential weaknesses, predictable defaults, and verbose error messages.
objectives: Analyze the authentication endpoint error messages.
Identify valid usernames through differential error responses.
Authenticate using standard default administrative credentials.
Access the admin console and capture the flag.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Try testing common corporate administrative usernames like 'admin', 'administrator', or 'manager'.
hint2: Notice that entering an invalid username says 'User does not exist', while an existing username says 'Incorrect password'.
hint3: Test common default corporate passwords for user 'admin' (e.g. 'admin', 'admin123', 'password', 'cyberflex2026').

title: That's Not My Account
scenario: Customers can view their invoices and receipts by clicking on orders in their dashboard. The application relies on user-supplied identifier parameters to fetch records.
objectives: Log in as regular customer 'john.doe'.
Inspect the order receipt URL or API request.
Tamper with the sequential order/user ID to view confidential orders belonging to another client.
Extract the confidential flag from the unauthorized invoice.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Look at the order details link: notice the parameter like ?id=1 or /api/orders/1.
hint2: What happens if you change the order ID number to 2, 3, or a higher sequential integer?
hint3: Order #3 contains a high-value confidential enterprise security contract. Retrieve it to find the flag.

title: Forged Request
scenario: When placing an order or updating profile tiers, client-side forms contain hidden or editable parameters specifying prices, discounts, and roles. The server blindly trusts client values without server-side validation.
objectives: Inspect the checkout or profile tier update request payload in browser developer tools.
Modify the unit price or requested role parameter before sending.
Successfully purchase a restricted $5,000 enterprise hardware key for $1 or elevate tier.
Capture the invoice flag generated for the manipulated transaction.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Open Developer Tools (F12) -> Network tab when submitting a purchase or updating profile.
hint2: Notice the JSON payload contains `price` or `role`. Can you intercept or send a custom POST request with price: 0.01?
hint3: Send a POST to /api/orders with {"productId": 4, "customPrice": 1.00, "quantity": 1} to trigger the purchase receipt flag.

title: The Untrusted Upload
scenario: Cyberflex provides an avatar and document submission feature. The upload filter only checks client-supplied headers or trivial file extensions, allowing dangerous files to be saved directly to a publicly accessible folder.
objectives: Investigate allowed file types on the file upload portal.
Test file extension and MIME type bypass techniques.
Upload a script or HTML payload to the uploads directory.
Access the uploaded file via the web browser to trigger execution and retrieve the flag.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Check what extensions the client form asks for and what the server validates in the request.
hint2: Try uploading an HTML or SVG file containing an embedded script, or examine how filename sanitization behaves.
hint3: Upload a file with a .html or .svg extension containing an XSS flag request, or access /uploads/ to read the uploaded payload flag.

title: Walking Through the Files
scenario: The document viewer feature allows customers to download terms of service, technical datasheets, and user manuals through a query parameter. The filename is concatenated directly to the filesystem path without path normalization.
objectives: Examine the document download URL: /api/documents/view?file=manual.pdf.
Attempt directory traversal using relative dot-dot-slash sequence (../).
Read the internal configuration file (e.g. server/config/secret.key or database/schema.sql).
Extract the confidential server flag.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Test if you can access parent directories by supplying ../ in the ?file= parameter.
hint2: Try accessing sensitive application files, such as /api/documents/view?file=../../package.json or internal config files.
hint3: Request: /api/documents/view?file=../../server/config/secret.key to read the server secret key containing the flag!

title: The Forgotten Endpoint
scenario: The development team upgraded the public API from v1 to v2. However, legacy v1 debug routes were never decommissioned and remain active without authentication.
objectives: Discover active API version endpoints.
Enumerate endpoints under /api/v1/ and /api/v2/.
Discover the unauthenticated legacy user export route.
Dump the legacy customer records to obtain the flag.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Modern APIs often use versioning such as /api/v1/ or /api/v2/.
hint2: Look for common administrative or debug endpoints like /api/v1/debug, /api/v1/export, or /api/v1/users.
hint3: Send a GET request to /api/v1/legacy/export-users to dump the legacy customer data containing the flag.

title: Trust the Token?
scenario: Cyberflex uses JSON Web Tokens (JWT) for authentication in certain microservices. The token verification implementation accepts the 'none' algorithm and uses a weak, easily brute-forced secret key.
objectives: Obtain a valid user JWT from the token login endpoint.
Decode the JWT header and payload.
Forge an administrative JWT using 'alg': 'none' or cracking the weak secret 'secret123'.
Present the forged token to access the restricted executive report.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Inspect the Authorization header or session token. It consists of three base64url-encoded parts separated by dots.
hint2: Try changing the 'alg' header field to 'none' and removing the signature portion, or sign it with the weak passphrase 'secret123'.
hint3: Submit a token with {"role":"admin","username":"admin"} signed with 'secret123' or alg 'none' to /api/jwt/admin-report.

title: The Missing Protection
scenario: The profile email update and credit transfer endpoints do not implement anti-CSRF tokens or SameSite cookie protection. An attacker can create an external form that forces an authenticated user's browser to execute state changes.
objectives: Inspect the profile update form and verify the absence of CSRF tokens.
Identify the vulnerable state-changing POST endpoint (/api/user/update-email).
Trigger the simulated CSRF verification proof of concept.
Confirm the unauthorized state change and receive the flag.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Check if requests to update user information require a unique, unpredictable token.
hint2: Notice that session cookies are sent automatically by the browser without any CSRF validation header.
hint3: Test the CSRF proof-of-concept generator or trigger an automated cross-origin state change to receive the flag.

title: Behind the Command
scenario: The Cyberflex administrative network tools include a host ping/traceroute diagnostic utility. User input is concatenated into an internal command runner. The command runner operates in a tightly sandboxed lab context for safe education.
scope: Only this local Cyberflex laboratory. Tightly sandboxed inside the application.
objectives: Access the network diagnostics tool in the administrative section.
Observe how host arguments are passed to the diagnostic utility.
Inject command separators (e.g. ; or &&) to execute simulated diagnostic inspection commands.
Read the diagnostic flag safely within the sandboxed lab context.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory. Sandboxed execution only.
hint1: Look at the Diagnostic Ping tool. How does it pass the host to the system?
hint2: Try appending command chaining operators like `127.0.0.1; whoami` or `127.0.0.1 && cat flag.txt`.
hint3: Send `127.0.0.1; cat flag.txt` or `127.0.0.1 & dir` into the diagnostic target field.

title: Chain Reaction
scenario: Real-world attackers rarely rely on a single flaw. In this mission, an IDOR flaw allows you to view an internal employee's profile, revealing a secret recovery PIN. Using that PIN, you can reset the administrator session and access the confidential audit vault.
objectives: Identify an IDOR vulnerability in the employee directory API.
Extract the hidden password reset PIN of administrator 'admin'.
Submit the reset PIN to take over the administrative account.
Access the high-security audit vault to capture the flag.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Query /api/users/profile?id=1 to view the internal employee profile of the administrator.
hint2: Inspect the returned JSON object for an internal recovery PIN or security question answer.
hint3: Use the discovered PIN at /api/auth/reset-password to reset admin password, log in, and access the audit vault.

title: API Breach
topic: Mass Assignment & Broken Object Level Authorization
scenario: The modern customer profile update API accepts a raw JSON document and maps all attributes directly to the database user record without property whitelisting. An attacker can inject privileged properties.
objectives: Inspect the PUT/POST request sent when saving profile bio and contact information.
Identify properties that should not be student-editable (e.g. 'role', 'is_verified', 'balance').
Send a modified JSON payload injecting {"role": "admin", "is_verified": 1}.
Verify account elevation and retrieve the enterprise API breach flag.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Inspect the request body sent to /api/v2/users/update when saving your bio.
hint2: Try adding extra fields to the JSON payload, like {"role": "admin"} or {"balance": 999999}.
hint3: Update your profile with {"role": "admin"} via /api/v2/users/update, then visit /api/admin/executive-stats to get the flag.

title: The Admin Problem
scenario: The Cyberflex administrative menu options are hidden in the browser UI for regular users. However, the backend maintenance API endpoints do not verify user role authorization before performing privileged operations.
objectives: Review client-side JavaScript files for hidden or commented administrative endpoints.
Attempt direct invocation of /api/admin/system-maintenance while logged in as a normal user.
Execute an administrative configuration dump.
Locate the maintenance master flag.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Search client-side scripts in public/js/ for references to '/api/admin/'.
hint2: Even if the UI hides the button, does the server actually verify that req.user.role === 'admin' on all endpoints?
hint3: Make a POST request directly to /api/admin/system-maintenance with your regular user session cookie.

title: Full Security Assessment
scenario: Cyberflex Industries has requested a black-box penetration test against their customer support ticket attachment service. No specific vulnerability hints are provided. You must conduct reconnaissance, locate the security flaw, demonstrate business impact, and recover the flag.
objectives: Perform black-box testing against the support ticket messaging system.
Identify an authorization bypass allowing access to internal attachments.
Retrieve the confidential executive briefing attachment.
Capture the assessment flag and prepare a finding summary.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Examine how support ticket attachments are referenced: /api/support/tickets/:id/attachments.
hint2: Ticket #99 is marked internal. Check if you can access its attachments or query ticket records without ownership checks.
hint3: Request /api/support/tickets/99/attachments to read the confidential executive attachment flag.

title: Find the Unknown
scenario: A legacy promotional coupon calculator in the billing checkout module contains an obscure business logic flaw. Under specific conditions, entering negative coupon quantities or stacking expired codes results in an account credit overflow.
objectives: Test promotional discount validation under unusual inputs.
Supply negative quantity or boundary discount values to the checkout endpoint.
Cause a balance overflow or obtain the enterprise tier for free.
Unlock the unknown zero-day discovery flag.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Test the coupon validation field at checkout with unexpected strings and negative integers.
hint2: What happens if you apply coupon 'DISCOUNT-NEG' or send a negative quantity like -1 in an order?
hint3: Submitting promo code 'OVERFLOW2026' or applying negative quantities triggers the billing logic flaw and returns the flag.

title: Final Assessment
scenario: This is your final capstone challenge. You must combine reconnaissance, authentication bypass, authorization tampering, and sandboxed privilege escalation to extract the ultimate Cyberflex Master Penetration Tester Flag. All prior skills will be required.
objectives: Perform full-scope assessment of the Cyberflex Industries portal.
Identify the restricted disaster recovery endpoint /recovery/master-backup.
Bypass the legacy header validation using internal proxy headers.
Extract the capstone master flag.
rules: Do not attack systems outside this laboratory.
hint1: Check the comments in /admin.html and inspect proxy headers accepted by the server.
hint2: The disaster recovery route checks for header 'X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1' or 'X-Cyberflex-Internal: true'.
hint3: Send a GET request to /recovery/master-backup with header 'X-Cyberflex-Internal: true' and admin session to obtain the capstone flag.

title: Defensive Mode — Patch The Application
scenario: Security isn't just about breaking applications; it's about fixing them. In this defensive exercise, you will review the vulnerable source code of the SQL injection and Path Traversal modules, apply secure coding patches (parameterized queries and path resolution validation), and verify that the exploits are neutralized.
objectives: Review the vulnerable code snippet.
Activate the secure patch toggle in the Defensive Portal.
Re-run the exploit to verify that the attack vector is blocked.
Capture the remediation verification flag.
rules: Authorized laboratory testing only.
hint1: Navigate to defensive.html to review the vulnerable versus patched code snippets.
hint2: Toggle the SQL injection or Path traversal patch to ON.
hint3: Submit the patch verification test to receive the defensive master flag.
